name: Fish
title: Fish (4.0)

presenceList.meta: R1, Ec1, Ec3, G1, G2, G3, Q3

type.text: **Values are strings with no declaration**: `set x 10` and `set x abc` are the same operation, and nothing states what a name holds
**No sum types**: An option that may be absent, numeric, or textual is a list of words, and the reader decodes the convention from the calling code
**No generics**: A function is specialised only by its positional arguments, so the same logic is written again for each shape of data

**One namespace for every name**: Functions and variables share one flat space, so collisions are avoided by convention — the `__fish_`-prefixed helper names in the bundled completions are the visible result (T6, T11)
**An unset name expands to an empty list**: `set -q` tests whether a name is set, but nothing forces it to be, so a mistyped variable silently expands to nothing
**Lists are values, not strings to be re-split**: `set a 1 2 3` and `$a` expand to exactly three arguments, so element structure survives expansion without quoting

construction.text: **Global is still the default**: An assignment without a scope flag reaches the innermost existing scope or the global one, so an accidental write into the caller is easy
**No immutability by default**: There is no read-only binding, so any visible name can be reassigned
**`set -l` gives block scope**: A variable declared local inside a function, a `begin`/`end` block, a `for`, a `while`, or an `if` disappears at the end of that block
**`alias` is sugar over `function`**: An alias becomes a real function, so the invocation name and the body are separated instead of textually substituted
**`argparse` validates options at the boundary**: A function declares its own option spec, so callers do not hand-roll a `getopts` loop and a bad option fails before the body runs
**Configuration lives outside scripts**: `~/.config/fish/config.fish`, the `conf.d/*.fish` snippets, and the universal-variable file separate shell setup from script logic

memory.text: **No allocation syntax**: There is no pointer, no address, and no `free`; lists and strings are allocated by the interpreter
**Block scope bounds a value's lifetime**: A `set -l` list is released at the end of its block, so storage does not leak past the code that created it
**Export joins a list on the way out**: A list assigned to an exported variable is joined with `:`, so `PATH` is edited as a list without building a string by hand
**Assignment copies the list**: `set b $a` duplicates every element, and there is no way to reference a list without copying it
**Command substitution is materialised whole**: `(cmd)` builds the entire output before the enclosing command runs, so a large output is held in memory
**Universal variables outlive the process**: `set -U` writes to `fish_variables`, so a value persists after the shell exits until it is erased deliberately

error.text: **No structured error path**: A command reports success through `$status` and text on stderr; there is no exception and no error value
**Errors are not composable**: `and` and `or` chain status codes, but a status carries no payload and cannot be returned from a function as data
**A non-zero status is easy to ignore**: A function reports the status of its last command, so a failure in the middle of a block is discarded unless `or return` follows it
**`$pipestatus` reports every stage**: Each stage of a pipeline keeps its own status, so a failure is not hidden by a successful last stage

**Syntax errors are reported with a source position**: Fish names the file, line, and column, but only for text it has parsed, so a fault inside a function body is reported when the function is defined
**An unknown command is a hookable event**: `fish_command_not_found` runs when a command is missing, so the message can be replaced, but the failure remains a status code

concurrency.text: **No concurrency primitives**: There is no thread, lock, channel, or await; the only parallel construct is backgrounding with `&`
**Event handlers decouple producer from consumer**: `function --on-variable NAME`, `--on-event`, `--on-process-exit`, and `emit` let a consumer subscribe without the producer knowing it exists
**Processes are the unit of parallelism**: Concurrency is expressed with pipes and background jobs, so no shared address space has to be reasoned about
**Process events are the only synchronisation**: A script coordinates jobs by watching exit events or by `wait`, and no value can be returned from a job
**Background jobs share the environment**: A `&` job inherits every global and universal variable, so ordering between jobs is unspecified unless the script waits
**No coprocess**: Fish cannot keep a two-way conversation with a child, so an interactive child must be driven through files or a `while read` loop

platform.text: **Not a POSIX shell**: Fish does not implement the POSIX shell language, so a `#!/bin/sh` script is a different language and `sh -c` calls a separate program
**One implementation defines the language**: With no standard to satisfy, behaviour is fixed by the fish manual and its release notes
**Runs on every Unix-like target**: Fish ships on Linux, the BSDs, and macOS, and is packaged by every major distribution
**Windows support is through an emulation layer**: Fish relies on Unix APIs and their semantics, so Windows use goes through WSL, Cygwin, or MSYS2 rather than a native port
**One implementation is one point of failure**: There is no second implementation to test the language's contract against
**fish is the default login shell nowhere**: A user installs it and sets it as their shell, so availability depends on the host's configuration
**It is not a POSIX shell**: A fish script runs only under fish, so portable system scripts, `configure` scripts, and `#!/bin/sh` entry points cannot be written in fish

performance.text: **Interpreted with no compilation**: Every command is parsed and executed as text, and fish offers no ahead-of-time path
**The core is native code**: Fish was written in C++ through the 3.x series and was ported to Rust for 4.0, so parsing, expansion, and completion run in compiled code rather than in script
**Command substitution does not re-split**: `(cmd)` performs no word splitting or globbing, so a large result is not re-parsed argument by argument
**Start-up can be profiled and trimmed**: `fish --profile-startup` measures configuration work and `--no-config` skips it
**Start-up runs the configuration snippets**: An interactive shell sources `config.fish` and every file in `conf.d`, so a heavy prompt or completion setup costs time on each new shell
**`for` over a substitution materialises the output**: A large `(cmd)` result is held in memory before the loop starts

ecosystem.text: **No package manager in the language**: There is no dependency resolver, so plugins are copied into `~/.config/fish` by third-party managers such as Fisher or Oh My Fish
**The ecosystem is small but growing**: Completions and prompt themes exist for popular tools, and there are far fewer fish libraries than `sh` libraries
**The bundled completion system is large**: `complete -c` declarations ship with fish and cover hundreds of commands, so everyday completion needs no add-on
**`fish_config` gives a built-in UI**: Prompts and themes are edited in a browser against files under `~/.config/fish`
**Documentation is first-class**: The manual, the tutorial, and `help <builtin>` are maintained with each release
**Third-party plugin managers own the plugin ecosystem**: Fisher and Oh My Fish are unofficial, so the plugin supply chain is not part of the language

evolution.text: **No breaking-change culture**: Fish adds features and documents the few incompatible changes in the release notes
**Release notes record every incompatibility**: The manual lists removals and behaviour changes for each version, so an upgrade is inspectable
**The project ships on a regular cadence**: Fish 4.0 was released in February 2025, and further 4.x releases followed it
**No standards body**: The direction of the language follows its maintainers rather than a committee
**Non-POSIX means the language may keep diverging**: With no standard to align to, fish is free to change and is not compelled to hold `sh` semantics

domain.text: **Strong for interactive work**: Syntax highlighting, autosuggestions, and completion make the terminal the primary domain
**Good for personal automation on a fixed host**: Where the interpreter is guaranteed, a fish script is shorter and clearer than its `sh` equivalent
**Lists map to the filesystem naturally**: `$PATH` and command output are lists of paths, and `path` and `string split` operate on them directly
**Weak for distribution**: A fish script cannot be shipped to a host without fish, which rules fish out for bootstrap, packaging, and installer code
**Not a general-purpose language**: The model is a shell over external commands, so real data processing moves to other tools

learning.text: **The tutorial and manual are written for newcomers**: Fish ships a tutorial and an FAQ, and each builtin has its own help page
**Error messages name the file, line, and column**: A beginner sees where the problem is rather than a bare failure
**The language is smaller and more regular than `sh` or `zsh`**: One `end` closes every block, `set` is the only binding command, and there is no word splitting to learn
**Quoting habits from other shells misfire**: `"$var"` and `[ -f x ]` do not apply, and `$var` is not split where an `sh` user expects it to be
**The builtin vocabulary is large**: `string`, `math`, `path`, `set`, `argparse`, `complete`, and `status` each carry their own option set

syntax.text: **No word splitting means fewer quotes**: `$var` expands as written, so a path containing a space needs no quoting to survive
**One binding form**: There is no `=`, no `setenv`, and no `typeset` to choose between
**`and` and `or` begin a line**: A boolean continuation puts the operator at the start of the next command, which reads unusually
**Piping a block needs a wrapper**: A multi-command producer must be written as `begin ... end` before it can be piped
**`switch` has no fallthrough**: A case ends at the next `case`, so an intentional fallthrough must be written as a second case

testing.text: **No test framework in the language**: A test is a function that calls the code and checks `$status`, with no assertion or reporting facility
**Debugging is `breakpoint` and `fish_trace`**: Fish can pause with `breakpoint` and print a stack with `status stack-trace`, but it has no debugger with breakpoints, stepping, and inspection
**Faults appear only on the branch that runs**: With no static check, a mistyped variable or a bad list index is found during the run
**`fish --no-execute` checks syntax without running**: A script can be parsed before it is executed
**`fish_indent --check` fails on unformatted code**: A shipped formatter gives a cheap consistency gate in a test path
**`fish --private` isolates a test from user state**: Configuration, history, and universal variables are left untouched, so a test run is reproducible

security.text: **Text can re-enter the interpreter**: Input assembled from untrusted data and passed to `eval`, or interpolated into a substituted command, becomes code
**No word splitting removes a whole class of injection**: An unquoted `$var` does not split or glob, so a value with spaces or `*` cannot become several arguments or an unexpected path list
**`string escape` and `string collect` make quoting explicit**: Output can be quoted for re-input instead of being concatenated by hand
**`argv` and `argparse` keep options out of the parser**: A function receives its arguments as a list, so a value beginning with `-` is not silently taken as an option
**No memory-safety surface**: Lists and strings are interpreter-managed, so a fish script has no buffer to overflow
**History and universal variables are unencrypted state**: Command history and `set -U` values are written to disk in the user's configuration, so a secret typed at the prompt is recorded by default

governance.text: **Semantics rest on the implementation**: POSIX defines the standard sh-family shells, not this one, and no conformance suite exists

tradeoffs: **Fish is deliberately not POSIX**: Giving up `sh` compatibility buys the design freedom that removes word splitting and most quoting noise
**Universal variables are a convenience with a lifecycle cost**: Persisting a value outside the shell trades reproducibility for ergonomics
**Aliases became functions because functions are better**: The change breaks the textual-substitution habit from other shells, which is the point of the change
**The web-based configuration UI is a front end**: `fish_config` writes plain files under `~/.config/fish`, so the browser is not a runtime dependency
**Autosuggestions and highlighting are interactive features**: They cost start-up work and terminal capability, and they are not part of the scripting language
**The Rust port is an implementation change**: The language contract is unchanged; the gain is in the codebase, not in what a script may rely on
verdict: Fish lowers the coupling that a scripting shell normally imposes on construction and on text handling: `set -l` gives block scope, `$var` never splits, lists are first-class, and functions replace textual aliases. Its core score still stops at 43, because the value model has no types, every name is global by default, and an error remains a status code rather than a value. The price is paid elsewhere: fish is not a POSIX shell, so a fish script runs only where fish is installed, and start-up configuration, an unofficial plugin supply chain, and the absence of a test framework hold the platform and ecosystem score to 49.

energy.text: Every operation starts a process: time, and therefore energy, is dominated by process startup.

ai-readiness.text: Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [@joel2025lowresource].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

delivery.note: The installed interpreter reads the source at run time; no compiled unit crosses a boundary
